scenes.title: Leaving Tangier
scenes.caption: In 1325, he left Tangier to make the pilgrimage to Mecca and visit Medina. He recalled setting out without a companion and finding the separation from his parents difficult.

scenes.title: Rest beside the road
scenes.caption: At Bijaya, he developed a fever but decided to continue. A companion advised him to sell his donkey and heavy baggage so that he could travel more lightly.

scenes.title: A place in the caravan
scenes.caption: In Tunis, he joined the caravan travelling to the Hijaz and was chosen as its judge. The party left in November 1325, following the North African coast toward Tripoli.

scenes.title: The road beside the sea
scenes.caption: He followed the coastal road toward Tripoli with the pilgrimage caravan. For part of the journey, mounted escorts and archers accompanied the travellers to protect them from raiders.

scenes.title: Alexandria’s lighthouse
scenes.caption: At Alexandria, he entered the lighthouse and found one side already ruined. He described its high doorway and the wooden bridge that gave access to the interior.

scenes.title: Cairo from the water
scenes.caption: Cairo impressed him with its size, crowds and traffic on the Nile. From the river, he would have seen boats carrying passengers and supplies along the city’s waterfront.

scenes.title: The city at walking pace
scenes.caption: He described Cairo as a crowded city with many markets. In its lanes, he would have encountered food sellers, porters and residents buying their daily provisions.

scenes.title: A boatman’s equipment
scenes.caption: On the Nile, boatmen would have used wooden steering oars, fibre ropes and cloth sails. These fittings needed regular adjustment and repair during everyday river travel.

scenes.title: Shade in Damascus
scenes.caption: In Damascus, he visited the Umayyad Mosque and admired its architecture. Its courtyard and arcades provided spaces for worship, teaching and rest within the busy city.

scenes.title: Water for the road
scenes.caption: Before leaving Damascus for the Hijaz, the caravan would have prepared water and provisions for the desert. Leather waterskins could be carried on pack saddles and refilled along the route.

scenes.title: Approaching Medina
scenes.caption: He travelled to Medina to visit the Prophet’s mosque and tomb, one of his purposes in leaving Morocco. The town stood among date-palm gardens in an otherwise dry landscape.

scenes.title: Among the pilgrims
scenes.caption: He reached Mecca for his first hajj in 1326. His account describes the sanctuary, the Kaaba and the practices of the pilgrims who gathered there.

scenes.title: The markets near the shrine
scenes.caption: In Najaf, he passed through markets for food, fruit, cloth and perfumes on his way to the shrine of Ali. He also described a college where visitors received bread, meat and dates for three days.

scenes.title: Waterways of Basra
scenes.caption: At Basra, he travelled by a small boat toward Ubulla. He described a waterway lined with gardens and date palms, with settlements connected by boats.

scenes.title: Fruit in Isfahan
scenes.caption: He praised Isfahan’s apricots, quinces, grapes and melons. Although he found much of the city damaged by fighting, he described orchards, streams and pigeon towers on the approach.

scenes.title: An orchard outside Shiraz
scenes.caption: He described Shiraz as a well-built city surrounded by orchards and crossed by streams. He travelled there especially to meet the scholar Majd al-Din Ismail.

scenes.title: Baghdad across the Tigris
scenes.caption: In Baghdad, he found inhabited quarters alongside extensive ruins. His account describes the city on both sides of the Tigris, where boats linked the riverbanks.

scenes.title: At the jewellers’ stalls
scenes.caption: At Tabriz, he visited the jewellers’ bazaar and was struck by the ornaments and precious stones on display. He also described the fine clothing worn by the women who came to buy there.

scenes.title: Weight and workmanship
scenes.caption: At the jewellers’ stalls in Tabriz, balances and small tools would have been used to weigh and work precious materials. Such equipment supported the trade in the ornaments he admired.

scenes.title: Staying to learn
scenes.caption: After further travels, he returned to Mecca and remained there to study. Lessons and conversations with scholars were an important part of his time in the city.

scenes.title: Taking ship at Jeddah
scenes.caption: He reached Jeddah after his stay in Mecca and took ship on the Red Sea. At the port, passengers and supplies would have been transferred to vessels preparing to sail south.

scenes.title: A passage under sail
scenes.caption: During the Red Sea passage, the crew would have adjusted the sail and rigging as the wind changed. He recalled difficult winds and the discomforts of this early sea journey.

scenes.title: Aden beneath the rock
scenes.caption: He described Aden as a busy trading port in a hot, dry setting. Ships arrived from India, and its merchants depended on trade across the Indian Ocean.

scenes.title: A guest at the meal
scenes.caption: In Mogadishu, he was received as a guest and served several meals a day. His account gives particular attention to the large portions and the hospitality shown to visiting merchants.

scenes.title: What is set before a guest
scenes.caption: His description of meals in Mogadishu includes rice and accompanying dishes. Bowls and shared serving vessels would have been part of the hospitality he experienced there.

scenes.title: An island’s green edge
scenes.caption: He described Mombasa as an island with fruit trees and well-built wooden mosques. Bananas and fish were important foods, while grain had to be brought from elsewhere.

scenes.title: Kilwa from the channel
scenes.caption: He admired Kilwa as a well-built town and praised its ruler’s generosity. Approaching by sea, he would have seen waterfront buildings and the vessels serving this trading settlement.

scenes.title: The groves outside Dhofar
scenes.caption: Outside Dhofar, he saw banana groves, coconut palms and betel vines. He recorded the size and sweetness of the bananas, and described betel climbing on cane supports or up the palms.

scenes.title: Water for an island port
scenes.caption: At Hormuz, he noted that fresh water was valuable. He described residents fetching it from wells and rainwater reservoirs outside the town, then carrying it back by boat.

scenes.title: Welcomed at the lodge
scenes.caption: In Anatolia, he often stayed with the Akhi brotherhoods, whose members offered travellers food and lodging. At Konya, he encountered this network of local hospitality again.

scenes.title: A room made ready
scenes.caption: At an Anatolian lodge, guests would have found mats or rugs, lamps and food prepared by their hosts. Such rooms supported the hospitality he repeatedly described along this part of the route.

scenes.title: Waiting to sail at Sinop
scenes.caption: At Sinop, he waited about forty days for sailing weather. After hiring a Greek vessel, he waited another eleven days for a favourable wind before crossing the Black Sea.

scenes.title: Bells above the harbour
scenes.caption: At Caffa, he heard church bells and visited a harbour crowded with vessels. He described the town as a major Genoese trading port with busy markets.

scenes.title: A city on the move
scenes.caption: He described Özbeg Khan’s travelling camp as a large settlement of tents and wagons. The court, its households and their belongings moved together across the steppe.

scenes.title: Wood, wheel and felt
scenes.caption: In the Golden Horde, he travelled in wagons and described portable dwellings. Wooden wheels, frames and felt coverings would have required regular maintenance on long journeys.

scenes.title: Across the Golden Horn
scenes.caption: He visited Constantinople while accompanying Princess Bayalun. His account describes a city divided by water, with churches, markets and a separate settlement across the Golden Horn.

scenes.title: Through the broken arcade
scenes.caption: In Bukhara, he found a once-celebrated centre of learning badly damaged. He described ruined mosques, colleges and markets left by the Mongol conquest.

scenes.title: A city with empty spaces
scenes.caption: He praised Samarkand’s size and setting but also recorded ruined buildings. The city he passed through combined surviving neighbourhoods with areas still damaged by earlier conquest.

scenes.title: Across the Hindu Kush
scenes.caption: On the way toward India, he crossed the Hindu Kush. He described the difficulty of travelling through the cold mountain country with pack animals and supplies.

scenes.title: Waiting at the gate
scenes.caption: After crossing the Indus, he reached Multan and waited to continue to Delhi. Officials there handled the arrival of foreign visitors seeking the sultan’s court.

scenes.title: Before the sultan
scenes.caption: In Delhi, Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq appointed him as a judge. He described elaborate court ceremonies, generous rewards and the risks of losing the ruler’s favour.

scenes.title: Listening to a case
scenes.caption: He spent several years serving as a judge in Delhi. In that role, he would have heard petitions and disputes, working with other officials and religious scholars.

scenes.title: Gifts at court
scenes.caption: He received money, clothing and other gifts while seeking and serving court patrons. Such exchanges helped support his travels but also tied him to the rulers who employed him.

scenes.title: Ships waiting offshore
scenes.caption: At Calicut, he found Chinese ships preparing for the eastward voyage. His account describes thirteen large vessels in the port and the smaller craft that served them.

scenes.title: A closer look at the junks
scenes.caption: He described the Chinese ships at Calicut in some detail, including their mat sails, large oars and wooden cabins. He identified China as the place where these vessels were built.

scenes.title: After the storm at Calicut
scenes.caption: He was ashore when the storm struck Calicut. Two ships were wrecked, while the vessel carrying his belongings sailed away; he was left unable to continue the embassy as planned.

scenes.title: Life at the lagoon
scenes.caption: In the Maldives, he lived among island households and served as a judge. Fishing, coconut products and travel between islands would have been part of the daily life around him.

scenes.title: A hull takes shape
scenes.caption: In the Maldives, wooden boats connected the inhabited islands. Builders would have used local timber and coconut-fibre cordage when constructing and maintaining these vessels.

scenes.title: Small things that travel far
scenes.caption: He noted the importance of cowrie shells and coconut fibre in the islands’ trade. Cowries circulated as money elsewhere, while fibre from coconut husks was made into useful cordage.

scenes.title: The ascent
scenes.caption: In Sri Lanka, he climbed the mountain associated with the sacred footprint. He described steep sections where chains helped travellers make the ascent.

scenes.title: Bengal by boat
scenes.caption: In Bengal, he travelled through river country and visited the religious teacher Shah Jalal. He described plentiful, inexpensive food and settlements linked by waterways.

scenes.title: A waterfront in the rain
scenes.caption: In Samudra, he stayed as a guest before continuing toward China. Around the port, timber buildings and covered landings would have sheltered people and cargo during rain.

scenes.title: Conversation after prayer
scenes.caption: He met Samudra’s sultan at the mosque. After prayer, the ruler sat with scholars to discuss religious questions, an exchange that continued into the evening.

scenes.title: A forest of masts
scenes.caption: His account describes Zaytun, usually identified as Quanzhou, as an exceptionally large port. He noted the many junks at anchor and the smaller vessels gathered around them.

scenes.title: Canals in Hangzhou
scenes.caption: His account describes al-Khansa, generally identified as Hangzhou, as an immense city. Canals, bridges and closely built waterfront neighbourhoods would have shaped travel through it.

scenes.title: Packing for the westward sea
scenes.caption: On the return from China, he stopped at Samudra again and stayed with its ruler. He then continued west toward India before beginning the longer journey back to Morocco.

scenes.title: Land after the long crossing
scenes.caption: On his westward return, he reached Dhofar after crossing from India. He then continued toward Hormuz and the route through Persia.

scenes.title: A city prays together
scenes.caption: During the plague in Damascus, he witnessed a public gathering for prayer. He described Muslims, Christians and Jews taking part with their sacred books.

scenes.title: The Nile again
scenes.caption: After his last pilgrimage, he returned to Cairo on the way west. From Egypt, he continued to Alexandria and took ship toward North Africa.

scenes.title: The lighthouse, twenty-three years later
scenes.caption: When he returned to Alexandria in 1349, he found the lighthouse much more ruined than before. He reported that it was no longer possible to enter it or reach its doorway.

scenes.title: Back in Fez
scenes.caption: After returning to Tangier in 1349, he travelled to Fez and the Marinid court. He had been away from Morocco for roughly twenty-four years.

scenes.title: Granada and the Alhambra
scenes.caption: He visited Granada during the reign of Yusuf I and praised the gardens, orchards and streams around the city. Its hillside neighbourhoods would have offered views across the Darro valley toward the Alhambra.

scenes.title: Before the desert opens
scenes.caption: At Sijilmasa, he bought camels and provisions for the Sahara crossing. He praised the town’s dates and stayed with a local scholar before joining the southbound caravan.

scenes.title: Walls made of salt
scenes.caption: At Taghaza, he found buildings made from salt slabs and a settlement supported by salt mining. Caravans carried the salt south to markets beyond the desert.

scenes.title: Shelter beyond the sands
scenes.caption: Walata was his first major stop after crossing the Sahara. In its houses, he would have found shaded rooms, mats and water vessels suited to everyday life in the hot climate.

scenes.title: Waiting at the court
scenes.caption: He stayed for several months at the court of Mansa Sulayman. His account describes public audiences, attendants, clothing and the formal behaviour expected around the ruler.

scenes.title: A river passage to Gao
scenes.caption: From Timbuktu, he travelled toward Gao in a boat hollowed from a single piece of wood. He called the river the Nile, although this part of his journey followed the Niger.

scenes.title: Copper rods at Takedda
scenes.caption: At Takedda, he described copper production and rods of different thicknesses used in exchange. The pieces circulated locally as a means of payment.

scenes.title: A journey becomes a book
scenes.caption: After his return to Fez, he dictated his travels to Ibn Juzayy at the sultan’s request. The resulting work, known as the Rihla, was completed in 1355.
